expectedText:
LAST WILL AND TESTAMENT
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Alameda County

DECLARATION
I, Jordan Alex Lee, a resident of Alameda County County, California, declare this to be my Last Will and Testament, and I revoke all prior wills and codicils I have made.

TESTAMENTARY CAPACITY
For this will to be valid, Jordan Alex Lee must have testamentary capacity at the time it's signed: sufficient mental capacity to understand that this is a will, to understand and recall the nature and extent of Jordan Alex Lee's own property, and to remember and understand Jordan Alex Lee's relationships with living family members and others affected by the will. Capacity can also be defeated a second way, independent of the general test: a mental health disorder involving delusions or hallucinations that actually caused a specific distribution decision the testator wouldn't otherwise have made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An individual is not mentally competent to make a will if, at the time of making the will, either of the following is true: (1) The individual does not have sufficient mental capacity to be able to do any of the following: (A) Understand the nature of the testamentary act. (B) Understand and recollect the nature and situation of the individual’s property. (C) Remember and understand the individual’s relations to living descendants, spouse, and parents, and those whose interests are affected by the will. (2) The individual suffers from a mental health disorder with symptoms including delusions or hallucinations, which delusions or hallucinations result in the individual’s devising property in a way that, except for the existence of the delusions or hallucinations, the individual would not have done."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6100.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the two-part testamentary capacity test (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6100.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual legal test for capacity — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. The two paths to incapacity are independent: a testator can meet the general understand-and-recall test yet still have a specific gift invalidated if it's shown to be the product of a delusion, and this statute doesn't override other evidence rules already used to prove incapacity generally. A conservator can make a will for a conservatee only with specific prior court authorization — this document doesn't cover that separate process. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 6100.5(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

HOW THIS WILL MUST BE SIGNED
For this will to be valid, it must be signed by Jordan Alex Lee (or by someone else in Jordan Alex Lee's presence and at Jordan Alex Lee's direction), and witnessed by at least two people who are present at the same time, who each watch Jordan Alex Lee sign or acknowledge the will, and who understand that what they're signing is Jordan Alex Lee's will.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The will shall be signed by one of the following: (1) By the testator. (2) In the testator’s name by some other person in the testator’s presence and by the testator’s direction. (3) By a conservator pursuant to a court order to make a will under Section 2580. (c) (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), the will shall be witnessed by being signed, during the testator’s lifetime, by at least two persons each of whom (A) being present at the same time, witnessed either the signing of the will or the testator’s acknowledgment of the signature or of the will and (B) understand that the instrument they sign is the testator’s will."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6110(b)-(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, signature and witness requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6110.)
  "If a will was not executed in compliance with paragraph (1), the will shall be treated as if it was executed in compliance with that paragraph if the proponent of the will establishes by clear and convincing evidence that, at the time the testator signed the will, the testator intended the will to constitute the testator’s will."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6110(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the harmless-error exception for a defectively executed will (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6110.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual execution requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. A will that misses one of these formalities isn't automatically void: if the person offering the will can show by clear and convincing evidence that the testator intended the document to be their will at the time they signed it, the will can still be treated as validly executed. That's a real, but demanding, safety net — clear and convincing evidence is a higher bar than the ordinary preponderance standard used in most civil disputes. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 6110) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

THE HANDWRITTEN-WILL ALTERNATIVE
A completely different kind of will exists under this same state's law: a will that doesn't meet the signature-and-witness requirements above can still be valid as a holographic will — with no witnesses required at all — if its signature and its material provisions are in the testator's own handwriting. A holographic will that doesn't state the date it was signed carries a real risk: if that missing date creates doubt about whether it or a different will controls, the undated holographic will loses to the other one unless it can be shown to have been signed later — and if there's a real question about whether the testator had capacity at some point during the possible window it was signed, the undated will is invalid unless it's shown to have been signed while the testator had capacity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A will that does not comply with Section 6110 is valid as a holographic will, whether or not witnessed, if the signature and the material provisions are in the handwriting of the testator."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6111(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, holographic will validity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6111.)
  "If a holographic will does not contain a statement as to the date of its execution and: (1) If the omission results in doubt as to whether its provisions or the inconsistent provisions of another will are controlling, the holographic will is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency unless the time of its execution is established to be after the date of execution of the other will. (2) If it is established that the testator lacked testamentary capacity at any time during which the will might have been executed, the will is invalid unless it is established that it was executed at a time when the testator had testamentary capacity."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6111(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the risk of an undated holographic will (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6111.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a lower-formality alternative genuinely exists — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will, and not a recommendation to use it instead of a properly witnessed will. This document is a witnessed will under the requirements described above, not a holographic one; this clause explains the alternative path for context, since a testator who later handwrites informal notes about their estate could unintentionally create a second, competing holographic will. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 6111) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

SPECIFIC GIFTS
I give the following specific items or amounts to the following people or organizations:

_______________________________________________ to _______________________________________________
_______________________________________________ to _______________________________________________
(Add additional lines as needed.) If any of these named beneficiaries doesn't survive me by 120 hours, that gift instead becomes part of my residuary estate, described below, unless I've stated a different result above.

RESIDUARY ESTATE
I give the rest of my estate — everything not specifically given above — to Jordan Alex Lee's spouse, Morgan Lee. If Jordan Alex Lee's spouse, Morgan Lee doesn't survive me by 120 hours, my residuary estate instead passes to: _______________________________________________.

EXECUTOR
I nominate Morgan Lee to serve as executor of this will. If Morgan Lee is unable or unwilling to serve, I nominate Casey Lee to serve instead. I waive the requirement that my executor post a bond.

WHAT HAPPENS WITHOUT A NAMED EXECUTOR
This will names an executor below because naming one is what actually controls who administers Jordan Alex Lee's estate. If no executor is named, or the named executor and any alternate are unwilling or unable to serve, the court appoints an "administrator with the will annexed" instead — chosen, by default, from the same statutory order of priority used when there's no will at all: starting with a surviving spouse or domestic partner, then children, then more distant relatives, and eventually creditors or any other person, well down the list. That default order isn't absolute, though: a person who takes something under the will has priority over a person who doesn't, and a person who takes more than half the estate's value under the will has priority over other people who'd otherwise share that same priority category.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An administrator with the will annexed shall be appointed as personal representative if no executor is named in the will or if the sole executor or all the executors named in the will have waived the right to appointment or are for any reason unwilling or unable to act."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8440 (California Legislative Information text), when an administrator with the will annexed is appointed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8440.)
  "(a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), persons and their nominees are entitled to appointment as administrator with the will annexed in the same order of priority as for appointment of an administrator. (b) A person who takes under the will has priority over a person who does not, but the court in its discretion may give priority to a person who does not take under the will if the person is entitled to a statutory interest that is a substantially greater portion of the estate than the devise to the person who takes under the will and the priority appears appropriate under the circumstances. A person who takes more than 50 percent of the value of the estate under the will or the person's nominee, or the nominee of several persons who together take more than 50 percent of the value of the estate under the will, has priority over other persons who take under the will."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8441(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), the priority order applied, and the will-beneficiary override (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8441.)
  "Subject to the provisions of this article, a person in the following relation to the decedent is entitled to appointment as administrator in the following order of priority: (a) Surviving spouse or domestic partner as defined in Section 37. (b) Children. (c) Grandchildren. (d) Other issue. (e) Parents. (f) Brothers and sisters. (g) Issue of brothers and sisters. (h) Grandparents. (i) Issue of grandparents. (j) Children of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (k) Other issue of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (l) Other next of kin. (m) Parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (n) Issue of parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (o) Conservator or guardian of the estate acting in that capacity at the time of death who has filed a first account and is not acting as conservator or guardian for any other person. (p) Public administrator. (q) Creditors. (r) Any other person."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8461 (California Legislative Information text), the underlying statutory priority order for appointment as administrator, applied here through § 8441(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8461.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory fallback — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This priority order is exactly why naming an executor (and at least one alternate) matters even for a modest estate: without it, administration defaults to whoever the statute favors, which may not be the person the testator would have chosen — and even that default order can itself be displaced by who actually takes property under the will.

BOND REQUIREMENT — AND HOW TO WAIVE IT
Unless waived, state law requires an appointed executor to post a bond — approved by the court, and conditioned on faithfully carrying out the job — before the court will actually issue them the authority to act. This will waives that requirement, which the law specifically allows a will to do; without a waiver in the will (or a written waiver signed by every beneficiary), the executor has to post one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as otherwise provided by statute, every person appointed as personal representative shall, before letters are issued, give a bond approved by the court."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8480 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the default bond requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8480.)
  "A bond is not required in either of the following cases: (1) The will waives the requirement of a bond. (2) All beneficiaries waive in writing the requirement of a bond and the written waivers are attached to the petition for appointment of a personal representative. This paragraph does not apply if the will requires a bond."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8481 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, how the bond requirement is waived (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8481.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default requirement and a genuine waiver mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. A waiver in the will isn't absolute: a court can still require a bond anyway, on request or on its own motion, for good cause — so an executor shouldn't assume a waiver in this document guarantees no bond will ever be required. Both citations below are from different statutory sections (§ 8480 and § 8481), each supporting a distinct part of this claim.

GUARDIAN FOR MINOR CHILDREN
If I have a minor child at the time of my death and a guardian is needed, I nominate Riley Lee to serve as guardian of the person and estate of that child. If Riley Lee is unable or unwilling to serve, I nominate Sam Lee to serve instead.

NOMINATING A GUARDIAN FOR A MINOR CHILD
Jordan Alex Lee can nominate a guardian of the person, the estate, or both, for a minor child in this will — but that nomination only actually controls in specific circumstances: either the other parent joins in or consents in writing to the same nominee, or, at the time a guardianship petition is actually filed, the other parent is dead, lacks the legal capacity to consent, or their consent wouldn't be required for the child to be adopted.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Subject to Section 1502, a parent may nominate a guardian of the person or estate, or both, of a minor child in either of the following cases: (a) Where the other parent nominates, or consents in writing to the nomination of, the same guardian for the same child. (b) Where, at the time the petition for appointment of the guardian is filed, either (1) the other parent is dead or lacks legal capacity to consent to the nomination or (2) the consent of the other parent would not be required for an adoption of the child."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1500 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, when a parent's guardian nomination controls (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1500.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine legal mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific nomination, and not a guarantee that a court will follow it. A nomination in a will isn't self-executing — it takes effect only through an actual guardianship proceeding, and a court can still decline to appoint the nominee if doing so wouldn't serve the child's best interest. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1500); no additional independent source was found for this.

HOW THIS WILL CAN BE REVOKED
Jordan Alex Lee can revoke this will, in whole or in part, in one of two ways: by a later will that revokes it expressly or by conflicting with it, or by burning, tearing, canceling, obliterating, or destroying it (personally, or by someone else in Jordan Alex Lee's presence and at Jordan Alex Lee's direction) with the specific intent of revoking it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A will or any part thereof is revoked by any of the following: (a) A subsequent will which revokes the prior will or part expressly or by inconsistency. (b) Being burned, torn, canceled, obliterated, or destroyed, with the intent and for the purpose of revoking it, by either (1) the testator or (2) another person in the testator’s presence and by the testator’s direction."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6120 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the two methods of revoking a will (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6120.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, exclusive methods of revocation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. A physical act (burning, tearing, and so on) done accidentally, or by someone without the testator's direction, doesn't revoke a will — the intent to revoke is what matters, not just the physical damage. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 6120); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHAT A LATER DIVORCE DOES TO THIS WILL
If Jordan Alex Lee's marriage is later dissolved or annulled, that alone automatically revokes — unless this will expressly says otherwise — any gift to the former spouse, any power of appointment given to the former spouse, and any nomination of the former spouse as executor, trustee, conservator, or guardian. Property that would have gone to the former spouse instead passes as though the former spouse died before Jordan Alex Lee. If Jordan Alex Lee later remarries the same former spouse, the revoked provisions come back into effect.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless the will expressly provides otherwise, if after executing a will the testator’s marriage is dissolved or annulled, the dissolution or annulment revokes all of the following: (1) Any disposition or appointment of property made by the will to the former spouse. (2) Any provision of the will conferring a general or special power of appointment on the former spouse. (3) Any provision of the will nominating the former spouse as executor, trustee, conservator, or guardian."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6122(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, automatic revocation of former-spouse provisions on divorce (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6122.)
  "If any disposition or other provision of a will is revoked solely by this section, it is revived by the testator’s remarriage to the former spouse. (c) In case of revocation by dissolution or annulment: (1) Property prevented from passing to a former spouse because of the revocation passes as if the former spouse failed to survive the testator. (2) Other provisions of the will conferring some power or office on the former spouse shall be interpreted as if the former spouse failed to survive the testator."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6122(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, revival on remarriage and treatment as predeceased (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6122.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, automatic default — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. A legal separation that doesn't actually terminate marital status is not a "dissolution" for this purpose, so a will's provisions for a separated-but-still-married spouse aren't automatically revoked by a separation alone. No other change in circumstances — the birth of a child aside from the separate omitted-child protections, a falling out with a beneficiary, and so on — automatically revokes any part of a will under this statute; a testator who wants a different result has to actually update the will. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 6122) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

A SPOUSE MARRIED AFTER THIS WILL WAS SIGNED
If Jordan Alex Lee marries someone after signing this will and never updates the will to provide for that spouse, the law doesn't simply let the omission stand — the omitted spouse is entitled by default to a share of the estate: half of the community and quasi-community property, plus a share of separate property equal to what the spouse would have received had there been no will at all, capped at half the separate property in the estate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as provided in Section 21611, if a decedent fails to provide in a testamentary instrument for the decedent’s surviving spouse who married the decedent after the execution of all of the decedent’s testamentary instruments, the omitted spouse shall receive a share in the decedent’s estate, consisting of the following property in said estate: (a) The one-half of the community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 100. (b) The one-half of the quasi-community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 101. (c) A share of the separate property of the decedent equal in value to that which the spouse would have received if the decedent had died without having executed a testamentary instrument, but in no event is the share to be more than one-half the value of the separate property in the estate."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21610 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the omitted spouse's default share (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21610.)
  "The spouse shall not receive a share of the estate under Section 21610 if any of the following is established: (a) The decedent's failure to provide for the spouse in the decedent's testamentary instruments was intentional and that intention appears from the testamentary instruments. (b) The decedent provided for the spouse by transfer outside of the estate passing by the decedent's testamentary instruments and the intention that the transfer be in lieu of a provision in said instruments is shown by statements of the decedent or from the amount of the transfer or by other evidence. (c) The spouse made a valid agreement waiving the right to share in the decedent's estate. (d) (1) If both of the following apply: (A) The spouse was a care custodian, as that term is defined in Section 21362, of the decedent who was a dependent adult, as that term is defined in Section 21366, and the marriage commenced while the care custodian provided services to the decedent, or within 90 days after those services were last provided to the decedent. (B) The decedent died less than six months after the marriage commenced. (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), a spouse described by this subdivision shall be entitled to receive a share of the estate pursuant to Section 21610 if the spouse proves by clear and convincing evidence that the marriage between the spouse and the decedent was not the product of fraud or undue influence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21611 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, when the omitted-spouse share doesn't apply (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21611.)
  "“Dependent adult” means a person who, at the time of executing the instrument at issue under this part, was a person described in either of the following: (a) The person was 65 years of age or older and satisfied one or both of the following criteria: (1) The person was unable to provide properly for his or her personal needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter. (2) Due to one or more deficits in the mental functions listed in paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (a) of Section 811, the person had difficulty managing his or her own financial resources or resisting fraud or undue influence. (b) The person was 18 years of age or older and satisfied one or both of the following criteria: (1) The person was unable to provide properly for his or her personal needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter. (2) Due to one or more deficits in the mental functions listed in paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (a) of Section 811, the person had substantial difficulty managing his or her own financial resources or resisting fraud or undue influence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21366 (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of "dependent adult" used by the care-custodian carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21366.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, automatic protection — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. This default share doesn't apply in several real situations: if the will itself shows the omission was intentional; if the testator provided for the new spouse outside the will (and meant that transfer to replace a provision in it); if the spouse signed a valid waiver of the right to share in the estate; or — a specific anti-abuse rule — if the spouse was a paid care custodian of a testator who was a legally defined "dependent adult" (broadly, someone 65 or older with certain functional or mental limitations, or 18 or older with substantial difficulty managing their own finances or resisting fraud or undue influence because of a mental deficit), the marriage began while the spouse was providing that care (or within 90 days after), and the testator died less than six months after the marriage, unless the spouse can prove by clear and convincing evidence that the marriage wasn't the product of fraud or undue influence. This document doesn't update itself to reflect a marriage after signing — a testator who marries after execution needs a new will or a codicil to actually provide for the new spouse, rather than relying on this default share.

A CHILD BORN OR ADOPTED AFTER THIS WILL WAS SIGNED
A child of Jordan Alex Lee who is born or adopted after this will is signed, and who isn't provided for in it, is entitled by default to a share of the estate equal to what that child would have received had there been no will at all. The same default share applies to a child alive when the will was signed whom Jordan Alex Lee left out only because Jordan Alex Lee believed the child was dead or didn't know about the child's birth. That default share doesn't apply if the decedent's failure to provide for the child was intentional and appears from the testamentary instruments, if the decedent had other children and left substantially all the estate to the omitted child's other parent, or if the decedent provided for the child by a transfer outside the will meant to replace a provision in it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as provided in Section 21621, if a decedent fails to provide in a testamentary instrument for a child of decedent born or adopted after the execution of all of the decedent’s testamentary instruments, the omitted child shall receive a share in the decedent’s estate equal in value to that which the child would have received if the decedent had died without having executed any testamentary instrument."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21620 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the omitted after-born or after-adopted child's default share (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21620.)
  "If, at the time of the execution of all of decedent’s testamentary instruments effective at the time of decedent’s death, the decedent failed to provide for a living child solely because the decedent believed the child to be dead or was unaware of the birth of the child, the child shall receive a share in the estate equal in value to that which the child would have received if the decedent had died without having executed any testamentary instruments."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21622 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, a child the testator believed dead or didn't know about (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21622.)
  "A child shall not receive a share of the estate under Section 21620 if any of the following is established: (a) The decedent's failure to provide for the child in the decedent's testamentary instruments was intentional and that intention appears from the testamentary instruments. (b) The decedent had one or more children and devised or otherwise directed the disposition of substantially all the estate to the other parent of the omitted child. (c) The decedent provided for the child by transfer outside of the estate passing by the decedent's testamentary instruments and the intention that the transfer be in lieu of a provision in said instruments is shown by statements of the decedent or from the amount of the transfer or by other evidence."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21621 (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, when the omitted-child share doesn't apply (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21621.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, automatic protection for an after-born or after-adopted child, and of the real, specific circumstances where that protection doesn't apply — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. This document doesn't update itself to reflect a child born or adopted after signing; the default share described here is a fallback for an unaddressed gap, not a substitute for a will that directly states what the testator wants for children born or adopted later.

IF A BENEFICIARY DIES AT NEARLY THE SAME TIME
Under this state's default rule, a beneficiary who doesn't outlive Jordan Alex Lee by at least 120 hours (five days) is treated as if they died before Jordan Alex Lee — so their gift passes as though they'd predeceased, not to their own estate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A person who fails to survive the decedent by 120 hours is deemed to have predeceased the decedent for the purpose of intestate succession, and the heirs are determined accordingly. If it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that a person who would otherwise be an heir has survived the decedent by 120 hours, it is deemed that the person failed to survive for the required period. The requirement of this section that a person who survives the decedent must survive the decedent by 120 hours does not apply if the application of the 120-hour survival requirement would result in the escheat of property to the state."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6403(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the 120-hour survival requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6403.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default survival requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. The burden runs against survival: if it can't be established by clear and convincing evidence that someone survived by the full 120 hours, they're deemed not to have survived. There's a real exception: this 120-hour requirement doesn't apply if enforcing it would cause the property to escheat to the state for lack of any other heir. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 6403(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

THE REAL LIMITS OF A NO-CONTEST CLAUSE
A clause disinheriting anyone who challenges this will is far narrower than it sounds: under this state's law, a no-contest clause can only be enforced against a direct challenge to the will's validity brought without probable cause, and — only if the clause expressly says so — against a challenge to a property transfer on the ground that the property wasn't the testator's to give, or against filing or pursuing a creditor's claim. Probable cause exists if the facts known to the person challenging, at the time they filed, would lead a reasonable person to believe there's a reasonable likelihood the challenge will succeed after a chance to investigate further.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A no contest clause shall only be enforced against the following types of contests: (1) A direct contest that is brought without probable cause. (2) A pleading to challenge a transfer of property on the grounds that it was not the transferor’s property at the time of the transfer. A no contest clause shall only be enforced under this paragraph if the no contest clause expressly provides for that application. (3) The filing of a creditor’s claim or prosecution of an action based on it. A no contest clause shall only be enforced under this paragraph if the no contest clause expressly provides for that application."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 21311(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Probate Code, the three narrow categories a no-contest clause can reach (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21311.)
  "For the purposes of this section, probable cause exists if, at the time of filing a contest, the facts known to the contestant would cause a reasonable person to believe that there is a reasonable likelihood that the requested relief will be granted after an opportunity for further investigation or discovery."

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21311(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the definition of probable cause
citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, probable cause exists if, at the time of filing a contest, the facts known to the contestant would cause a reasonable person to believe that there is a reasonable likelihood that the requested relief will be granted after an opportunity for further investigation or discovery.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the real, narrow scope of no-contest enforcement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will, and not a claim about whether including such a clause is a good idea. A beneficiary who challenges a will in good faith, with a genuinely reasonable basis, isn't automatically disinherited just because the challenge ultimately fails — the probable-cause safe harbor protects a good-faith challenge regardless of outcome. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 21311) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: If this will isn't contested, state law makes it easy to actually prove it in court years later: it can be proved on the testimony of just one of the two subscribing witnesses, not both, and that witness's evidence can be given by affidavit — with a copy of the will attached — rather than requiring them to appear in person.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8220 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, proving a will with one witness's affidavit
citations.quote: Unless there is a contest of a will: (a) The will may be proved on the evidence of one of the subscribing witnesses only, if the evidence shows that the will was executed in all particulars as prescribed by law. (b) Evidence of execution of a will may be received by an affidavit of a subscribing witness to which there is attached a photographic copy of the will, or by an affidavit in the original will that includes or incorporates the attestation clause.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, low-friction proof mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. This shortcut disappears entirely if the will is actually contested; it only applies to the routine case where no one is disputing that the will is genuine. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 8220); no additional independent source was found for this.
